guides.title: Making Soap: Saponification, Lye Math & Safety
guides.summary: How soap is made from fats and lye, with the chemistry of saponification, exact lye-calculation math using SAP values, and the safety discipline required to handle sodium hydroxide.

sections.heading: What Soap Is and the Saponification Reaction
sections.body:
Soap is the salt of a fatty acid. It is made by reacting a fat or oil (a triglyceride — three fatty-acid chains bonded to one glycerol backbone) with a strong alkali (a base), a reaction called SAPONIFICATION (Latin sapo = soap). The word equation is:

Fat/oil + Lye → Soap + Glycerol (glycerin)

Chemically, for sodium hydroxide:

Triglyceride + 3 NaOH → 3 R-COONa (soap) + C₃H₅(OH)₃ (glycerol)

Here R-COONa is the soap molecule: R is a long hydrocarbon chain (typically 12–18 carbons) that is OIL-LOVING (hydrophobic), and the -COONa (carboxylate) head is WATER-LOVING (hydrophilic). This dual nature is why soap cleans: the tails bury into grease while the heads face the water, forming tiny spheres called MICELLES that lift oil and dirt into rinse water.

Two alkalis are used. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH, 'caustic soda') makes HARD bar soap. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, 'caustic potash') makes SOFT or liquid soap. You cannot substitute one for the other without recalculating, because their molecular weights differ (NaOH = 40 g/mol, KOH = 56.1 g/mol).

sections.heading: SAP Values and the Core Lye Calculation
sections.body:
Every fat needs a specific amount of lye to fully react. This is captured by its SAP VALUE (saponification value): the milligrams of KOH needed to saponify 1 gram of that fat. Because manufacturers publish SAP for KOH, and most bar soap uses NaOH, you convert.

Step 1 — Get the SAP value for each oil (typical values, mg KOH per g):
• Olive oil: 190 (0.190 for NaOH after conversion below)
• Coconut oil: 257
• Palm oil: 199
• Tallow (beef fat): 200
• Lard (pork fat): 195
• Castor oil: 180

Step 2 — Convert KOH SAP to NaOH SAP by dividing by the mass ratio 56.1/40 = 1.403:

NaOH factor = (KOH SAP in mg/g) ÷ 1000 ÷ 1.403

Example: olive oil KOH SAP 190 → 190 ÷ 1000 = 0.190 g KOH per g oil → 0.190 ÷ 1.403 = 0.1354 g NaOH per g oil.

Step 3 — Multiply by oil weight:

Lye (g) = Oil weight (g) × NaOH factor

For 500 g olive oil: 500 × 0.1354 = 67.7 g NaOH at 0% superfat (full reaction).

sections.heading: Superfat, Lye Concentration & Water
sections.body:
SUPERFAT (or 'lye discount') means using slightly LESS lye than the full amount so a little unreacted oil remains, making the bar gentler and guaranteeing no leftover caustic lye. A 5% superfat is standard.

Superfatted lye = Full lye × (1 − superfat fraction)

For the olive-oil example at 5% superfat: 67.7 × 0.95 = 64.3 g NaOH.

WATER dissolves the lye into a solution. A common rule is a lye CONCENTRATION of 33% (i.e., lye is 33% of the lye-water solution by mass), which is safe and reliable:

Water (g) = Lye (g) ÷ 0.33 − Lye (g)

For 64.3 g lye: 64.3 ÷ 0.33 = 194.8 g solution; water = 194.8 − 64.3 = 130.5 g. A simpler beginner ratio is 'water = 2× lye by weight' (≈33.3% concentration), giving 128.6 g here — close enough.

Always work in mass (grams), never volume, because oils and lye have different densities. A digital scale accurate to 1 g is essential. NEVER guess lye amounts: too much leaves a caustic bar that burns skin; too much extra fat makes a soft bar that spoils (goes rancid).

sections.heading: Cold-Process Procedure, Step by Step
sections.body:
Cold process is the standard home method. For a 500 g olive+coconut blend (e.g., 350 g olive, 150 g coconut), recalc lye per oil and sum. Assume total lye 71 g, water 142 g for this illustration.

1. GEAR UP: goggles, chemical gloves, long sleeves, ventilation. Have a bottle of vinegar nearby (weak acid to neutralize splashes on surfaces — for skin, use lots of running water).
2. MIX LYE INTO WATER — ALWAYS add lye to water, never water to lye ('do like you oughta, add acid/alkali to water'). Adding water to solid lye can erupt. The solution self-heats to ~90 °C and releases fumes; stir gently, stand back, let cool to ~40 °C.
3. MELT OILS: warm solid oils (coconut) until liquid, then combine with liquid oils; cool to ~40 °C so lye and oils are within ~5–10 °C of each other.
4. COMBINE & BLEND: pour lye-water into oils, blend with a stick blender until 'TRACE' — the mix thickens to a thin-pudding consistency where drizzle leaves a fleeting trail on the surface. This means emulsification is complete.
5. ADD EXTRAS: at trace, mix in optional essential oils (~3% of oil weight = ~15 g) or colorants.
6. MOLD: pour into a silicone or lined mold; insulate with a towel for 24–48 h (it heats through a 'gel phase').
7. UNMOLD & CURE: cut into bars after 1–2 days; CURE on a rack 4–6 WEEKS. Curing lets water evaporate and saponification finish, yielding a harder, milder, longer-lasting bar.

sections.heading: Testing, Common Mistakes & Troubleshooting
sections.body:
TESTING FOR SAFETY: after cure, a properly made bar has a neutral-to-mild pH (~9–10). The old 'zap test' — briefly touching the tongue to the bar; a caustic bar 'zaps' like a 9-volt battery — indicates leftover lye and an unsafe bar (do this cautiously or use pH strips: >11 means unreacted lye, do not use).

COMMON MISTAKES:
• Wrong SAP or forgetting the KOH→NaOH conversion → lye-heavy, skin-burning bar.
• Measuring by volume instead of mass → wildly wrong ratios.
• Blending too hot → 'volcano' or cracking; too cold → false trace that separates.
• 'Ricing' (oils clump like rice grains) or 'seizing' (instant hardening) — usually from a reactive fragrance oil; work fast and pour anyway.
• SODA ASH (harmless white powder on the surface) from air contact — trim or steam it off.

TROUBLESHOOTING: an oily film or soft, weeping bar means too much superfat or too little lye — it may still be usable but rebatchable. A crumbly, brittle bar means too much lye or hard water — dangerous; discard.

sections.heading: Safety, Storage & Legal Notes
sections.body:
Sodium and potassium hydroxide are CORROSIVE: they cause chemical burns and permanent eye damage, and dissolve some metals (never mix or store lye in aluminum, tin, or zinc — they react and release flammable hydrogen gas; use stainless steel, heat-safe glass, or HDPE plastic).

SAFETY RULES:
1. Always wear splash goggles and gloves; lye burns are painless at first, so damage occurs before you feel it.
2. Mix in a ventilated area — the initial fumes irritate lungs; do not lean over the pot.
3. Add lye to water, slowly, stirring.
4. Keep children, pets, and food surfaces away; label lye containers clearly.
5. For skin contact: flush with copious cool running water for 15+ minutes. Do NOT smother a large lye burn in vinegar (the neutralization heat can worsen it); dilute with water first. Seek medical care for eye contact or serious burns — this guide is educational and not a substitute for professional treatment.

STORAGE: keep dry lye airtight (it absorbs water and CO₂ from air). Store finished soap somewhere dry and airy. Homemade soap is legal to make and use; selling cosmetics is regulated in many places (labeling, ingredient rules) so check local law before selling.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: Soapmaking is applied chemistry with real stakes — you're handling a caustic alkali — so the gear matters as much as the recipe. Here's what a first cold-process batch actually requires, none of it exotic:
ingredients: A digital kitchen or postal scale, accurate to 1 gram (or better, 0.1 g for small batches) — soap is always measured by weight, never volume, because oils and lye solution have different densities; any inexpensive electronics or kitchen-supply scale works.

100% pure sodium hydroxide (lye), sold as pellets, flakes, or micro-beads — check the label reads only 'sodium hydroxide,' since some hardware-store drain cleaners blend in aluminum chips or other additives that will react violently and ruin a batch. Soapmaking suppliers and some hardware stores carry the pure form.

A dedicated heat-resistant mixing pitcher for the lye solution — heavy PP #5 plastic, Pyrex-type borosilicate glass, or stainless steel. Never aluminum, tin, or non-anodized metals; lye corrodes them and can release flammable hydrogen gas.
Chemical-splash goggles (not everyday glasses) and elbow-length chemical-resistant gloves (nitrile or heavy rubber), since a lye splash in the eye or on skin needs to be flushed immediately.
A well-ventilated space — outdoors, a garage with the door open, or a kitchen with the exhaust fan and windows on — because dissolving lye releases a sharp fume for the first minute or so.
A stick (immersion) blender kept exclusively for soap, never returned to food use once it's touched lye.
Heat-safe silicone or stainless spatulas and a silicone or lined mold, again dedicated to soapmaking.
Two thermometers (or one, rinsed between uses) — an instant-read digital or a candy thermometer works, one to track the lye solution and one for the melted oils.

Your chosen oils and fats (olive, coconut, palm or a palm-free substitute, shea or cocoa butter, lard, tallow, etc.), from a grocery store or bulk food supplier, and distilled water from the same, since tap-water minerals can discolor a batch or throw off trace.
A spray bottle of plain household vinegar kept within arm's reach — it neutralizes lye on skin or a spill on contact and buys you time before rinsing.
A reliable lye calculator (an online tool or a printed SAP-value chart) to check every batch's math independently before you weigh a single gram — never trust a recipe you haven't verified yourself.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Calculating and Pouring a Test Batch
sections.body: The lye math in the previous sections only becomes intuitive once you've run it end to end on a batch small enough that a mistake costs you 500 grams of oil, not five kilograms. Here is a complete worked example — a 70% olive oil / 30% coconut oil bar at 5% superfat — followed by the physical pour.
steps: Pick a total oil weight and a blend. For this test batch: 500 g total oil, split 350 g olive oil (70%) and 150 g coconut oil (30%) — a classic beginner combination that balances olive oil's mild, conditioning lather against coconut oil's hardness and big bubbles.

Look up each oil's NaOH SAP value from a reference chart: olive oil ≈ 0.134 g NaOH per gram of oil, coconut oil ≈ 0.183 g NaOH per gram. Treat these as approximate — always cross-check against a current chart or calculator, since published values vary slightly by source and by the oil's exact fatty-acid batch.

Multiply each oil weight by its SAP value: 350 g × 0.134 = 46.9 g NaOH for the olive oil; 150 g × 0.183 = 27.45 g NaOH for the coconut oil. Add them: 46.9 + 27.45 = 74.35 g of NaOH would saponify all the oil with zero fat left over.

Apply your superfat discount. At 5% superfat you deliberately leave 5% of the oil un-saponified for skin-conditioning excess fat, so you use only 95% of the calculated lye: 74.35 g × 0.95 ≈ 70.6 g NaOH — round to 70.6 g on the scale.

Decide your water amount via a lye concentration. A beginner-friendly choice is a 33% lye concentration (NaOH is 33% of the combined lye-solution weight), which works out close to the traditional 'water = 2× the lye weight' rule of thumb: 70.6 g × 2 ≈ 141 g of distilled water.
Put on goggles and gloves, and set up outdoors or by an open window. Weigh out 70.6 g of NaOH and 141 g of distilled water separately.

Always add lye to water, never water to lye — pouring water into concentrated lye can cause violent, sputtering boiling. Sprinkle the NaOH slowly into the water while stirring; the solution will fume briefly and can shoot up to 180–200°F (82–93°C) in under a minute from the heat of dissolution alone. Set it aside to cool, away from pets and kids.

Melt and combine your 350 g olive oil and 150 g coconut oil in a heat-safe pot, warming just enough to fully liquefy the coconut oil (its melting point is about 76°F/24°C), then let both the oils and the lye solution cool to roughly 100–110°F (38–43°C) — close enough that neither shocks the other on contact.

Pour the lye solution into the oils (not the reverse) and blend with the stick blender in short bursts, alternating with hand-stirring, until the mixture thickens to 'trace' — a state where a drizzle from the blender leaves a visible trail on the surface for a second or two before sinking back in.
Pour immediately into your mold, tap it firmly on the counter to release air bubbles, and cover. Leave it undisturbed 24–48 hours to fully set before unmolding and cutting into bars.

Cure the bars on a rack with airflow for 4–6 weeks, turning occasionally. This isn't just water evaporating — saponification itself keeps completing slowly over this period, and the bars get measurably milder and longer-lasting the longer they sit.

Before calling the batch good, do a zap test (touch a cut bar briefly to your tongue) — a genuine electric tingle means free lye is still present and the bar needs more cure time or was under-measured on the oil side; a soapy, faintly bitter taste with no zap means it's done.

sections.heading: Fatty Acid Profiles: Why Olive Oil Soap and Coconut Oil Soap Feel Nothing Alike
sections.body: Every oil's soap-making behavior traces back to which fatty acids dominate its triglycerides, and each fatty acid contributes a specific, well-documented property to the finished bar. Lauric and myristic acids (the stars of coconut and babassu oil, together often over 60% of coconut oil's fatty acid content) saponify into salts that are extremely soluble and produce big, fast, fluffy lather — but they're also more aggressively cleansing, stripping natural skin oils if used at more than about 25–30% of a recipe. Oleic acid (monounsaturated, dominant in olive, canola, and high-oleic sunflower oils, often 65–80% of olive oil) saponifies into a soft, conditioning soap with a low, creamy lather and excellent mildness — it's why a 100% olive oil 'Castile' bar is famously gentle but takes months to fully harden and cure. Palmitic and stearic acids (saturated, dominant in palm oil, tallow, and cocoa/shea butter) contribute hardness and a stable, long-lasting bar, plus a dense, creamy lather rather than big bubbles. Linoleic and linolenic acids (polyunsaturated, found in soybean, sunflower, and hemp oil) condition well but oxidize readily once saponified, which is the leading cause of DOS ('dreaded orange spots') — rancid oxidation blotches that can appear on a cured bar months later if the recipe leans too heavily on high-linoleic oils. Soapmakers track this oxidative risk with a blend's iodine value (a measure of unsaturation: higher iodine value means more double bonds, softer soap, and shorter shelf life) and often keep a recipe's overall iodine value under about 70 for a bar that will store well for a year or more. Chemist and soap researcher Kevin Dunn popularized folding saponification value and iodine value into a single 'INS' number (roughly, SAP value minus iodine value) as a quick balance check — a blend with an INS in the neighborhood of 150–170 tends to produce a bar that is neither too soft (low INS, olive-oil-heavy) nor too hard and drying (very high INS, all coconut or palm) — though the number is a rough guide, not a substitute for actually testing a bar.

sections.heading: The Gel Phase: Heat, Color, and Why Some Soaps Turn Translucent
sections.body: Saponification is exothermic twice over, and both heat events matter for how a bar turns out. The first happens the instant lye touches water: dissolving NaOH releases roughly 44 kJ per mole into solution, which is why a concentrated lye solution can rocket from room temperature to 180–200°F (82–93°C) in under a minute — heat from simple dissolution, before a single molecule of oil has reacted. The second, gentler heat event unfolds over the following hours inside the mold, as the saponification reaction itself proceeds through the batch. If a freshly poured mold is insulated (wrapped in towels or set in a warm oven with the light on), the center can climb past 150–170°F (65–77°C) and pass through 'gel phase' — the soap turns glossy, translucent, and darker for several hours before cooling back to an opaque, matte finish. Gelled soap saponifies faster and more completely, often finishes curing sooner, and tends to show brighter, more saturated colors from any pigments used, because gel-phase heat helps colorants disperse evenly. Deliberately preventing gel — by pouring into a mold set in the refrigerator or freezer, or leaving it uninsulated in a cool room — instead yields a soft pastel, fully opaque bar throughout; this is standard practice for milk soaps, since the sugars in goat's milk or coconut milk will scorch and turn orange-brown (and can develop an unpleasant burnt smell) if the batch overheats during gel. Neither approach is 'wrong' — it's an aesthetic and formulation choice, not a safety one, as long as the batch is correctly measured to begin with.

sections.heading: Hot Process Soapmaking and Rebatching a Failed Batch
sections.body: Cold process, the method covered step by step earlier, lets saponification finish slowly over the following weeks at room temperature. Hot process soapmaking instead applies external heat — a slow cooker on low, or a double boiler — to drive the reaction to near-completion in a few hours, right in the pot. After reaching trace, the batch is cooked (typically 45 minutes to an hour), passing visibly through a translucent, petroleum-jelly-like 'vaseline stage' as saponification advances, then thickening into a mashed-potato-like paste that is glopped, rather than poured, into the mold. The payoff is that hot-process soap is technically usable almost immediately once it's cooled and hardened, since the lye has already been consumed in the pot — though a shorter cure of a week or two is still worth it to let water evaporate for a firmer, longer-lasting bar. Hot process also tolerates fragrance and botanical additions that would seize or discolor badly if exposed to a full cold-process cure, since they're stirred in right at the end rather than sitting through weeks of ongoing chemistry. Rebatching is the soapmaker's repair tool for a batch gone wrong — separated, grainy, poorly mixed, or simply forgotten before a fragrance was added. The cured or semi-cured soap is grated or chunked, returned to a double boiler or slow cooker with a splash of water, milk, or extra oil, and gently remelted until it can be stirred smooth and re-poured. Rebatching can rescue a batch that seized instantly at trace or one where the oils and lye never fully emulsified, but it cannot fix a genuinely miscalculated recipe — if the original lye amount was wrong, remelting it changes nothing about the chemistry already locked in, and the fix has to happen at the calculation stage, not the stove.

guides.title: Disinfectants & Water Chemistry: Chlorine & Iodine Doses
guides.summary: The chemistry of disinfecting water and surfaces with chlorine and iodine, including exact bleach and tablet doses, contact times, pH effects, and how to make a safe surface sanitizer.

sections.heading: First Principles: Disinfection vs Purification
sections.body:
DISINFECTION means killing or inactivating pathogenic microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, protozoa). It is not the same as making water chemically pure — disinfection targets living/infectious agents, not dissolved metals, salts, or chemicals. Key terms:

• PATHOGEN: a disease-causing microbe.
• CT VALUE: the product of disinfectant Concentration (mg/L, also written ppm — parts per million) × contact Time (minutes). CT = C × t. A given kill requires a minimum CT, so lower concentration needs longer time and vice versa.
• RESIDUAL: the leftover disinfectant remaining in water after demand is met, which keeps protecting against recontamination. For drinking water, a free chlorine residual of about 0.2–0.5 mg/L is a common target.
• TURBIDITY: cloudiness from suspended particles. Particles shield microbes and consume disinfectant, so always PRE-FILTER or settle cloudy water before chemical treatment; double the dose for cloudy or very cold water.

Chlorine and iodine both work by OXIDATION — they chemically attack microbial cell walls, enzymes, and genetic material. Neither reliably kills Cryptosporidium, a chlorine-resistant protozoan cyst; for that, use boiling or filtration.

sections.heading: Chlorine Chemistry and Free vs Combined Chlorine
sections.body:
When chlorine (as bleach) is added to water it forms HYPOCHLOROUS ACID (HOCl) and hypochlorite ion (OCl⁻):

NaOCl + H₂O → HOCl + Na⁺ + OH⁻

and HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻

HOCl is the powerful germ-killer — roughly 80–100× more effective than OCl⁻. The balance between them depends on pH (pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], a measure of acidity from 0–14, where 7 is neutral):
• At pH 6–7, ~75–96% is active HOCl → strong disinfection.
• At pH 8+, most converts to weak OCl⁻ → disinfection drops sharply.

So slightly acidic-to-neutral water disinfects far better. FREE CHLORINE = HOCl + OCl⁻ (available to kill). COMBINED CHLORINE = chlorine bound to ammonia/organics (chloramines), which is weak. CHLORINE DEMAND is the amount consumed by reacting with organic matter before any residual remains — dirty water 'eats' chlorine, so it needs more.

sections.heading: Exact Bleach Doses for Drinking Water
sections.body:
Standard unscented household bleach is sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl). CHECK THE LABEL concentration — it varies (commonly 5%, 6%, or 8.25%). Use only plain bleach: no scents, no 'splash-less', no added cleaners.

EPA/CDC emergency drinking-water guidance (for ~6% bleach):
• Clear water: 2 DROPS of 6% bleach per 1 liter (≈8 drops per US gallon).
• Cloudy/cold water: DOUBLE it — 4 drops per liter (≈16 per gallon). Pre-filter first.

Adjust for strength: for 8.25% bleach use ~2 drops per 2 liters (about half as much per volume). A common conversion: 1/8 teaspoon (≈8 drops) of 6% bleach treats about 4 liters (1 gallon) of clear water.

PROCEDURE:
1. Filter cloudy water through cloth and let settle.
2. Add the correct drops; stir.
3. Let stand 30 MINUTES (contact time). Longer for cold water (chlorine works slower below 10 °C).
4. The water should have a slight chlorine smell. If it does NOT, repeat the dose and wait another 15–30 min. If it still has no chlorine smell after two doses, discard — the demand is too high to trust.

WORKED EXAMPLE: You have a 10-liter jug of clear water and 6% bleach. Dose = 2 drops/L × 10 L = 20 drops (about 1/4 teaspoon). Stir, wait 30 minutes. Result: safe drinking water with a faint chlorine residual.

sections.heading: Iodine Dosing and Its Limits
sections.body:
Iodine (I₂) is an effective alternative, especially portable for travel. Forms and doses for 1 liter of clear water:

• IODINE TABLETS (tetraglycine hydroperiodide, e.g., 'Potable Aqua'): typically 1 tablet per liter; 2 for cloudy/cold. Wait 30 minutes (longer if cold).
• 2% TINCTURE OF IODINE (a medicine-cabinet antiseptic): 5 DROPS per liter of clear water; 10 drops if cloudy. Stir, wait 30 minutes.
• LUGOL'S / 5% solutions: use proportionally fewer drops (about 2 per liter) — always follow product instructions.

CONTACT TIME rises steeply in cold water: at 5 °C, wait 60+ minutes.

SAFETY/LIMITS — important:
1. Iodine is NOT for long-term use (more than a few weeks) because it affects the thyroid gland.
2. Do NOT use iodine if you are pregnant, have a thyroid disorder, or have a known iodine/shellfish allergy — consult a medical professional. This guidance is educational, not medical advice.
3. Iodine, like chlorine, does NOT reliably kill Cryptosporidium.
4. Iodine gives water a taste/color; a tiny pinch of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) added AFTER the contact time neutralizes taste and color (but only add it after disinfection is complete, or it will destroy the iodine's germ-killing action).

sections.heading: Making a Safe Surface Sanitizer
sections.body:
For sanitizing hard surfaces (not for drinking), a stronger chlorine solution is used, then air-dried.

HOUSEHOLD BLEACH SURFACE SANITIZER (approx 200–600 ppm free chlorine):
• General surfaces: ~1 tablespoon of 6% bleach per 1 gallon (≈4 L) of room-temperature water ≈ 200 ppm.
• Disinfecting after contamination: 1/3 cup of bleach per gallon (≈1900 ppm) for heavy jobs.

PROCEDURE: clean the surface of visible dirt first (organic matter consumes chlorine), apply solution, keep it WET for the required contact time (1–10 minutes depending on target; ~5 min is a safe default), then air-dry or rinse food-contact surfaces with clean water.

CRITICAL SAFETY RULES:
1. NEVER mix bleach with AMMONIA (many window/floor cleaners) — it releases toxic chloramine gas.
2. NEVER mix bleach with ACIDS (vinegar, toilet-bowl cleaner, some descalers) — it releases toxic chlorine gas.
3. Bleach solutions DEGRADE: mix fresh, use within 24 hours, store away from light and heat.
4. Ventilate the area and wear gloves; chlorine irritates skin, eyes, and lungs.

ALCOHOL alternative: a solution that is 60–70% ethanol or isopropanol by volume is an effective surface/hand sanitizer (below ~60% it is much weaker; above ~80% it evaporates too fast to work). This does not require water chemistry but must stay away from flame — alcohol vapor is flammable.

sections.heading: Physical Backup Methods & When Chemistry Fails
sections.body:
Chemistry has limits; know the physical fallbacks.

BOILING is the most reliable disinfection for pathogens (including Crypto and Giardia). A ROLLING BOIL for 1 MINUTE kills virtually all pathogens; at altitude above ~2000 m (6500 ft), boil for 3 MINUTES because water boils at a lower temperature (about 93 °C at 2000 m vs 100 °C at sea level — pathogens still die but need the longer time). Boiling does NOT remove chemicals, salts, or heavy metals.

SODIS (Solar Disinfection): fill a clear PET plastic or glass bottle with clear water and lay it in direct sun for 6 HOURS (or 2 days if cloudy). UV rays plus heat inactivate pathogens. Works only for clear water and won't remove chemicals.

FILTRATION: a filter rated at 1 micron (µm) or smaller removes protozoan cysts and most bacteria; only filters labeled for viruses (or paired with a chemical step) handle viruses, which are far smaller.

DECISION GUIDE:
1. Cloudy water → filter/settle first, always.
2. Suspect chemical/industrial contamination → chlorine/iodine will NOT help; use distillation or a specialized filter, or find another source.
3. Suspect Cryptosporidium (e.g., agricultural runoff) → boil or filter; don't rely on chlorine/iodine alone.
4. No fuel and no chemicals → SODIS.

Always store treated water in clean, covered containers to prevent recontamination, and keep a chlorine residual if possible for standing storage.

sections.heading: Equipment for Testing and Treating Water Yourself
sections.body: Doing your own dosing and verification — rather than just trusting a chart — takes a small, inexpensive kit:
ingredients: Plain, unscented household bleach labeled as sodium hypochlorite solution (typically 5–9% available chlorine), with no added fragrance, colorants, or 'splash-less' thickeners — those additives change the effective concentration and complicate dosing. Any grocery or hardware store carries a plain version.
A liquid medicine dropper or oral dosing syringe graduated in mL or drops, for precise small-volume dosing — pharmacies sell these cheaply, often free with liquid medication.
A chlorine test kit — either DPD drop-based or test strips, sold at pool-supply and hardware stores — that reads free and total chlorine in the 0–10 ppm range.
A pH test kit or digital pH meter/strips, also from a pool-supply or aquarium store, since chlorine's effectiveness depends heavily on the water's pH.
A 2% tincture of iodine bottle with its own built-in dropper, from a pharmacy, if you want to practice the iodine dosing method as well.
Clear glass or food-grade plastic containers of a known volume (1-liter measuring pitchers work well) so your dose calculations map directly onto a real quantity of water.
A basic liquid thermometer, since cold water needs longer contact times than the tables often assume.
A stopwatch or a phone timer, to hold yourself to the actual contact time rather than guessing.
Nitrile gloves, since concentrated bleach and iodine tincture will irritate skin with repeated contact.

A coffee filter, clean cotton cloth, or fine paper towel for pre-filtering cloudy water — chlorine and iodine both work far worse in turbid water, so clarifying first is part of the real procedure, not an afterthought.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Dosing, Timing and Verifying a Batch of Water
sections.body: This walks through actually running the bleach-dosing math from earlier in this guide on a real liter of water, then checking your own work with a test kit — the single best way to make the numbers stick.
steps: Draw exactly 1 liter of the water you intend to treat into a clear container. If it's visibly cloudy or has floating sediment, pre-filter it through a clean cloth or coffee filter first — disinfectant demand rises sharply in turbid water because chlorine reacts with suspended organic matter before it ever reaches a pathogen.
Check the bleach bottle's label for its percentage of available chlorine (commonly 6% for standard household bleach in most markets, sometimes 5% or 8.25%).

Using the dosing formula from the earlier section for 6% bleach, calculate the number of drops needed for 1 liter at a standard treatment target (roughly 2 drops of 6% bleach per liter for clear water, doubled to about 4 drops for cloudy water) — write the number down before you add anything.

Add the calculated number of drops with your dropper, counting out loud, then stir or shake the container thoroughly for about 30 seconds so the chlorine disperses evenly rather than pooling near the surface.

Check your water's temperature. If it's below about 10°C (50°F), extend the standard 30-minute contact time — cold slows the disinfection reaction considerably, and doubling the wait to 60 minutes is a reasonable field adjustment.
Start your timer and let the water stand, covered, for the full contact time — do not drink or taste it during this window.

At the end of the wait, smell the water: a faint, clean chlorine odor (like a lightly chlorinated pool) is the sign you dosed correctly. No smell at all suggests you under-dosed or the chlorine was consumed by contaminants; an overpowering bleach smell means you over-dosed.

Use your test kit to measure the free chlorine residual. A properly treated batch should read roughly 0.2–0.5 ppm free chlorine remaining after the contact time — this residual is your proof that enough chlorine survived contact with everything in the water to still be actively protecting it.

Check the pH strip or meter reading. If it's above about 8, note that your effective disinfection was weaker than the same dose at neutral pH (see below) — repeat the test at a slightly higher dose and compare the residual.

Repeat the whole test once using deliberately cloudy water (stir in a pinch of dirt) without pre-filtering, and once after filtering it — comparing the two final chlorine residuals is the clearest hands-on demonstration of why clarifying water before treating it matters as much as the dose itself.

sections.heading: Contact Time, CT Values, and Why Cold Water Needs More of Both
sections.body: Disinfection efficacy is not just about how much chlorine you add — it's the product of concentration and time, a relationship water engineers call the 'CT value' (concentration in mg/L multiplied by contact time in minutes). A given CT achieves a specific log-reduction of a specific pathogen, and different organisms require wildly different CTs to kill reliably. Ordinary bacteria and most enveloped viruses fall quickly to free chlorine, often needing a CT of only a few mg·min/L for a 99.9% (3-log) reduction. Giardia cysts are considerably tougher — EPA treatment guidelines call for a CT in the rough neighborhood of 100+ mg·min/L for 3-log inactivation at near-freezing water temperatures and neutral pH, which is exactly why field guidance settles on '1–2 ppm free chlorine held for 30 minutes' as a practical approximation of that CT for a person without a chemist's toolkit. Cryptosporidium oocysts are harder still — their thick outer wall makes them so chlorine-resistant that achieving a meaningful CT against them with household bleach alone would require either an impractically high dose or an impractically long wait, which is exactly why boiling or filtration is the recommended defense against Crypto rather than chlorine alone. Temperature is the other lever in the equation: the same chemical reaction that inactivates a pathogen slows down in cold water the same way any reaction rate does, so the CT tables water utilities use specify a much higher required CT at 0.5°C than at 25°C — often three to four times higher. In practice, this means a backpacker treating snowmelt at 3°C with the standard drop-count for 'clear water' is actually under-treating relative to summer stream water at 20°C unless the contact time is extended — hence the rule of thumb to double the wait in cold conditions rather than adding more chlorine, which can overshoot the taste threshold before it meaningfully improves the CT.

sections.heading: pH's Hidden Role: Why Chlorine Stops Working in Alkaline Water
sections.body: Free chlorine in water doesn't exist as one single species — it splits between hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and the hypochlorite ion (OCl⁻), and the ratio between them is entirely controlled by pH, following the equilibrium HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻ with a pKa around 7.5. This matters enormously because HOCl is the far more potent disinfectant of the two — commonly cited as somewhere between 40 and 80 times more effective at killing microorganisms than OCl⁻, because the neutral HOCl molecule can diffuse through a microbial cell wall far more readily than the charged ion can. At pH 6, water chemistry favors HOCl heavily (over 95% of the free chlorine present is in the active form); at pH 7.5, the split is roughly even; by pH 8.5, the balance has flipped hard toward the weaker OCl⁻ form, and the same ppm reading on a test strip is doing noticeably less disinfecting work. This is precisely why pool operators are told to hold pH between about 7.2 and 7.6 — not for swimmer comfort alone, but because letting pH drift upward silently wastes chlorine's killing power even while the free-chlorine number looks fine. For drinking-water treatment with household bleach, the standard drop-count guidance assumes roughly neutral source water; naturally alkaline water (common in limestone regions, or water that's had lime or soda ash added upstream) should either be dosed higher or given a longer contact time to compensate — and if you're testing pH anyway, treating water at pH 7 rather than pH 8+ gets you a materially safer margin for the identical chlorine dose.

sections.heading: Beyond Chlorine and Iodine: Chlorine Dioxide, Ozone, and Solar Disinfection
sections.body: Household bleach and iodine tincture are the two chemistries this guide focuses on because they're cheap, shelf-stable, and dosed with simple math, but they aren't the only chemical options, and each alternative trades off differently. Chlorine dioxide (ClO2) is sold commercially as two-part liquid drops or effervescent tablets that generate the gas in situ; unlike chlorine, it doesn't rely on the HOCl/OCl⁻ equilibrium and stays effective across a wider pH range, and it's markedly better than chlorine at inactivating Cryptosporidium — though even ClO2 needs several hours of contact time against Crypto specifically (commercial products often specify a 4-hour wait for that pathogen alone, versus 30 minutes for bacteria and viruses), so read the actual product instructions rather than assuming one contact time fits every organism. Ozone (O3) is an even stronger oxidizer than either chlorine species and is widely used in municipal treatment plants and bottled-water facilities, but it has no residual protection at all — it degrades back to oxygen within minutes of generation, so it must be produced on demand with an electrical ozone generator and used immediately, making it impractical without dedicated equipment. Solar water disinfection (SODIS) is the simplest non-chemical option: filling clear PET plastic bottles with water and leaving them in direct, unobstructed sunlight for a full six hours (or two consecutive days if the sky is cloudy) uses a combination of UV-A radiation and mild heating to damage pathogen DNA and proteins; it's endorsed by the World Health Organization as an emergency option for clear water, but it fails badly on turbid water (which blocks UV penetration) and, like ozone, leaves no residual — treated water can be recontaminated the moment it's poured into a dirty container. None of these replace the judgment calls the rest of this guide covers; they're additional tools for when chlorine's pH sensitivity, iodine's thyroid caveats, or a lack of contact time make one of the primary methods a poor fit for the water in front of you.

guides.title: Distillation, Extraction & Purifying Liquids
guides.summary: The physics of separating and purifying liquids: distillation and boiling points, condensation, solvent extraction, filtration, and building a simple still — with worked temperatures and safety.

sections.heading: Core Principles: Why Liquids Separate
sections.body:
Purifying liquids exploits differences in physical properties. The key terms:

• BOILING POINT (bp): the temperature at which a liquid's vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure and it turns to vapor throughout. Water boils at 100 °C at sea level (101.3 kPa); ethanol at 78.4 °C; salt does not boil at these temperatures (it stays dissolved and left behind).
• VAPOR PRESSURE: the pressure of vapor escaping a liquid's surface; higher vapor pressure = more VOLATILE (evaporates easily).
• CONDENSATION: cooling vapor back to liquid — the reverse of boiling.
• SOLUBILITY: how much of one substance dissolves in another (the SOLVENT). 'Like dissolves like' — polar solvents (water) dissolve polar/ionic substances (salt, sugar); non-polar solvents (oil, alcohol to a degree) dissolve non-polar substances (fats, many plant oils).
• MISCIBLE: two liquids that mix in all proportions (water + ethanol). IMMISCIBLE: liquids that separate into layers (oil + water), enabling separation by a separating funnel.

DISTILLATION separates liquids by boiling-point difference: heat the mixture, the more volatile component vaporizes first, then you condense that vapor separately. This purifies water from salt/minerals, and separates miscible liquids that boil at different temperatures.

sections.heading: Simple Distillation: Building a Basic Still
sections.body:
A distillation apparatus has three functional parts: a BOILING VESSEL (heated flask/pot), a CONDENSER (a cooled tube where vapor re-liquefies), and a COLLECTION VESSEL (receiver). A simple improvised still:

1. Boiling pot with a domed or angled lid so condensing droplets run to one side.
2. A tube (copper or food-grade) leading vapor from the pot out to a cooled coil.
3. The coil (the 'worm') sits in a bucket of cold water or has cold water running over it — this is the condenser.
4. Vapor cools in the coil, becomes liquid, and drips into a clean receiver.

For DESALINATING water (making fresh water from salty/dirty water): heat to a gentle boil (~100 °C), water vapor rises leaving salt, heavy metals, and most contaminants behind in the pot; the vapor condenses into pure DISTILLATE. Distillation removes salts, minerals, many chemicals, and pathogens (the heat kills them and they don't vaporize).

KEY POINT: do NOT boil violently — vigorous boiling flings tiny droplets of the dirty water ('carryover' or 'entrainment') into the vapor, contaminating the distillate. A slow, steady boil gives the purest product. A solar still (a sloped clear cover over a dark basin in the sun that condenses evaporated water onto the cover and drips it to a channel) uses the same principle without fuel, but produces only ~1–4 liters per day per square meter.

sections.heading: Fractional Distillation and Separating Mixed Liquids
sections.body:
When two miscible liquids have CLOSE boiling points, simple distillation gives a mixed, impure product. FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION improves separation using a FRACTIONATING COLUMN — a vertical column (often packed with beads, glass, or metal mesh) between the pot and condenser. As vapor rises and partly re-condenses many times on the packing, each cycle enriches the vapor in the more-volatile component. This is how petroleum refineries separate gasoline, kerosene, and diesel, and how laboratories separate solvents.

Worked concept — water/ethanol: ethanol boils at 78.4 °C, water at 100 °C. Heating a water/ethanol mix, vapor near 78 °C is ethanol-rich. However, there is an important limit: water and ethanol form an AZEOTROPE at about 95.6% ethanol by weight, a constant-boiling mixture (bp 78.2 °C) whose vapor has the SAME composition as the liquid — so ordinary distillation cannot push ethanol past ~95.6% purity no matter how many times you distill. Breaking an azeotrope needs special methods (drying agents, pressure changes). Note: distilling alcohol for consumption is legally restricted or illegal without a permit in many countries — this is included to explain the chemistry of azeotropes, not to instruct illegal production. The '95% cap' principle applies generally: azeotropes set purity ceilings for many liquid pairs.

sections.heading: Solvent Extraction: Pulling Compounds Out
sections.body:
EXTRACTION separates a desired compound by dissolving it selectively into a solvent it prefers, then removing the solvent.

LIQUID-LIQUID EXTRACTION uses two immiscible solvents. Example: to pull a water-insoluble compound out of a water mixture, shake it with an immiscible organic solvent; the compound partitions (distributes) into whichever layer it dissolves in best, governed by the PARTITION COEFFICIENT (the ratio of concentrations in the two solvents at equilibrium). Let the layers separate, then draw off the desired layer.

SOLID-LIQUID EXTRACTION (the everyday kind):
• INFUSION: steeping a solid in a solvent (tea leaves in hot water) to pull out soluble compounds. Concrete recipe: herbal infusion, ~1–2 g dried plant per 200 mL water at 90–100 °C for 5–10 minutes.
• DECOCTION: simmering tough material (roots, bark) to extract more — 20–45 minutes at a low boil.
• MACERATION / TINCTURE: soaking plant material in ethanol or a water/ethanol mix (e.g., 40% alcohol) for days to weeks; alcohol extracts compounds water can't. A common ratio is 1 part dried herb to 5 parts liquid by weight/volume.
• OIL INFUSION: extracting fat-soluble compounds into a carrier oil, gently warmed (~40–60 °C) for hours or at room temperature for weeks.

STEAM DISTILLATION extracts volatile plant oils (essential oils): steam passes through plant material, carries the volatile oils as vapor, then condenses; the oil (immiscible) separates from the water (the byproduct water is 'hydrosol'). This works below the oils' own boiling points, protecting heat-sensitive compounds. Note that any extract intended for consumption or skin use should be identity-verified and used cautiously; misidentified plants can be toxic — this is educational, not medical guidance.

sections.heading: Filtration, Decanting & Clarifying
sections.body:
Before or after distillation/extraction you often need to remove solids and cloudiness.

• DECANTING: letting solids settle, then carefully pouring off the clear liquid on top — simplest, no equipment.
• FILTRATION: passing liquid through a porous barrier that traps particles larger than its pores. Coffee filters or cloth catch coarse matter; laboratory filter paper is graded by pore size. For very fine clarification, add a FILTER AID like activated charcoal.
• ACTIVATED CHARCOAL (activated carbon): a highly porous carbon with enormous internal surface area (one gram can have 500–1500 m² of surface). It works by ADSORPTION — molecules stick to its surface — removing many organic chemicals, odors, colors, chlorine, and some toxins, but NOT salts, most heavy metals, or microbes. Layer it in a filter (sand → charcoal → cloth) for improvised water clarification, and always disinfect afterward, because charcoal does not kill pathogens.
• GRAVITY vs SUCTION: gravity filtration is slow but simple; pouring through a folded ('fluted') filter increases surface area and speed.

A robust improvised purification chain: (1) settle/decant, (2) filter through cloth + sand + charcoal to remove particles and some chemicals, (3) distill or disinfect to handle salts/pathogens. Each step targets a different contaminant class.

sections.heading: Safety, Energy & Common Errors
sections.body:
SAFETY:
1. HEAT & PRESSURE: never seal a heated distillation system fully — trapped vapor builds pressure and can explode. Always leave a vapor path/vent open to atmosphere.
2. FLAMMABILITY: alcohol and organic-solvent vapors are FLAMMABLE and can ignite from a nearby flame or spark. Distill volatile solvents far from open flame, ideally with electric heat and good ventilation.
3. BUMPING: a superheated liquid can suddenly erupt ('bump'); add BOILING CHIPS (small inert porous stones) or a stir to promote smooth, steady boiling.
4. TOXIC MATERIALS: distilling unknown liquids can concentrate toxins into the distillate OR the residue; do not distill mystery chemicals. Never distill toward the goal of making illegal, weaponizable, or toxic substances — keep to water, food, and safe extractions.
5. LEAD/ZINC: use food-grade tubing and vessels; some solders and galvanized (zinc) parts leach toxic metals into hot distillate — use copper, stainless steel, or food-grade glass/silicone.

COMMON ERRORS:
• Boiling too hard → carryover contaminates distillate.
• No condenser cooling → vapor escapes uncondensed, wasting product and posing a fire/scald risk.
• Forgetting the azeotrope limit → expecting 100% purity that distillation cannot reach.
• Using extraction solvents that dissolve the wrong things → poor yield; match solvent polarity to target ('like dissolves like').
• Skipping disinfection after charcoal filtration → microbially unsafe water.

ENERGY NOTE: distillation is energy-intensive because water's LATENT HEAT OF VAPORIZATION is high (~2260 kJ/kg — the energy to turn 1 kg of boiling water into steam). That is why distilling large volumes needs lots of fuel; solar stills trade speed for zero fuel cost.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Need to Build and Run a Still
sections.body: A basic distillation setup can be built from lab glassware or improvised from kitchen and hardware-store parts — here's what either route actually requires:
ingredients: A heat source you can control precisely — a laboratory hot plate is ideal, but a kitchen stove burner turned low works for a first build; avoid open flame directly under glass without a diffuser, since thermal shock can crack it.
A boiling vessel — a round-bottom flask from a lab/scientific supplier, or a repurposed stainless steel or enamel pot with a well-fitting lid for an improvised version.

A condenser — a glass Liebig or coil condenser from a lab supplier for a proper build, or a length of copper or food-grade silicone tubing run through a cold-water or ice bath for an improvised one. Avoid plain PVC tubing near heat; it can soften, deform, or leach into the vapor stream.

A thermometer (0–150°C range covers nearly everything here) mounted so its bulb sits in the vapor path near the take-off point, not down in the liquid — this is what tells you which fraction is currently coming over.
A means of sealing the joints — ground-glass fittings with a little vacuum grease for lab gear, or plumber's PTFE tape and a flour-and-water paste seal for an improvised rig.
Clean glass collection jars, and ideally two or three so you can separate the foreshot, the main run, and the tail without stopping to swap mid-stream.
A cold-water or ice bath for the condenser — a bucket or tray with a recirculating trickle of tap water is enough for casual use; ice water gives cleaner condensation on a hot day.
Chemical-splash goggles, heat-resistant gloves, and a nearby fire extinguisher rated for whatever heat source and liquids you're working with.
A secondary containment tray under the whole setup, so a cracked flask or a knocked-over jar doesn't spread liquid across a hot burner.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Distilling Purified Drinking Water at Home
sections.body: Distilling plain tap or well water is the safest and most forgiving first project — no flammable vapor, no toxic byproduct to worry about, just water and whatever's dissolved in it — and it's the best way to get a feel for the whole apparatus before distilling anything more complex.
steps: Fill your boiling flask or pot no more than two-thirds full with the water you intend to distill — leaving headspace prevents splashing over into the condenser during vigorous boiling.
Assemble the still: seat the thermometer so its tip sits level with the take-off arm (in the vapor path, not the liquid), connect the condenser, and check every joint is sealed.
Start your cold-water flow or fill the ice bath around the condenser before applying any heat — an unchilled condenser lets steam escape unrecovered.

Apply gentle heat and bring the water to a boil. At sea level you should see the thermometer settle right around 100°C (212°F); if you're at altitude, expect it lower — roughly 1°C less for every 300 m (1,000 ft) of elevation, so a Denver-altitude distillation (about 1,600 m) will read closer to 95°C.

Let the first small amount that condenses (a tablespoon or two) run into a separate discard jar — this 'foreshot' can carry the most volatile trace compounds dissolved in tap water and is standard practice to set aside rather than drink.
Swap in your main collection jar and let the bulk of the water distill over at a steady drip, keeping the heat low enough that the thermometer holds steady rather than climbing.

Watch the thermometer closely as the flask nears dryness — once most of the water has evaporated, the boiling point of whatever's left (concentrated minerals and any less-volatile residue) will start to climb measurably above 100°C. Stop heating as soon as you see that rise; boiling a flask fully dry cracks glass and scorches residue onto it.

Let everything cool fully before disassembling. Taste-test the collected water against the original — distilled water should taste noticeably flatter and 'emptier,' since the dissolved minerals that give tap water its taste were left behind in the flask.

Rinse the boiling flask and inspect the residue left behind — a visible ring of mineral scale is direct, tangible proof of what distillation actually removed, and a good comparison point if you repeat the process with water from a different source.

sections.heading: Steam Distillation and Pulling Essential Oils from Plants
sections.body: Many aromatic plant oils boil far too high (often well above 200°C) to ever distill directly without scorching or decomposing the plant material first, and simple distillation of the whole plant mash would just char it long before the oil ever vaporized. Steam distillation sidesteps this using a property of immiscible liquids: when two liquids that don't dissolve in each other are boiled together, the mixture boils once the sum of their two separate vapor pressures equals atmospheric pressure — not once either liquid alone reaches its own boiling point. Because water's vapor pressure is added to the oil's, the combination boils below 100°C, letting the essential oil ride over with the steam at a temperature far below where the oil would decompose on its own. Practically, this means passing steam through or over plant material (lavender flowers, rosemary, orange peel, and similar aromatics are classic examples) rather than boiling the plant directly in a pot of water, then condensing the mixed vapor exactly as in simple distillation. The condensate that collects is a two-layer liquid: the essential oil, generally less dense than water and immiscible with it, floats as a thin layer on top of the water below (called a hydrosol or 'flower water,' which itself is a valued byproduct in perfumery and cosmetics — rosewater is simply the hydrosol left over from rose steam distillation). A Florentine flask, which has a side spout positioned to draw off only the lower water layer while the oil layer stays behind, is the traditional tool for cleanly separating the two without needing a separate decanting step. Steam distillation for aromatics has ancient roots — the physician and polymath Ibn Sina (Avicenna) is widely credited with refining the technique for extracting rosewater and other plant essences around a thousand years ago, and the core principle he was exploiting is exactly the same partial-pressure chemistry taught in a modern general-chemistry course.

sections.heading: Azeotropes: Why You Can't Distill Some Mixtures to 100% Purity
sections.body: Fractional distillation, covered earlier in this guide, works by repeatedly re-vaporizing and re-condensing a mixture so the more volatile component keeps concentrating in the vapor with every pass — in principle, enough theoretical plates should be able to separate any two liquids down to arbitrary purity. In practice, some mixtures refuse to cooperate past a certain point, because they form an azeotrope: a specific composition at which the vapor coming off the liquid has exactly the same composition as the liquid itself. Once a distillation reaches that composition, there's nothing left for further plates to do — the vapor and liquid are identical, so no more separation occurs no matter how tall the column or how high the reflux ratio. The most commonly encountered example is ethanol and water, which form a minimum-boiling azeotrope at about 95.6% ethanol by weight, boiling at roughly 78.2°C — slightly below pure ethanol's own boiling point of 78.4°C. This is precisely why ordinary fractional distillation of a fermented wash can concentrate ethanol up to about 95–96% but never past it; getting to the 99.5%+ 'absolute' ethanol used in labs and some industrial processes requires breaking the azeotrope entirely, historically done by adding a third liquid (an entrainer, though older approaches are now avoided for toxicity reasons) to form a new, more separable three-component azeotrope, or with modern molecular sieves that selectively adsorb the remaining water molecules by physical pore size. Azeotropes aren't rare exceptions — many industrial solvent pairs form them at their own characteristic compositions — and recognizing that a still has hit one (temperature holds rock-steady well short of either pure component's boiling point, and further distillate composition stops changing) saves a lot of wasted effort chasing purity that plain distillation physically cannot deliver.

sections.heading: Reading a Boiling-Point (Vapor-Liquid Equilibrium) Diagram
sections.body: The theory behind fractional distillation's plate-by-plate enrichment is easiest to see on paper before you see it in glass. A vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) diagram plots temperature on the vertical axis against composition (mole or mass fraction of the more volatile component) on the horizontal axis, and for a well-behaved mixture it shows two curves that meet at each pure component's boiling point: a lower 'bubble point' curve (the temperature at which a liquid of that composition starts to boil) and an upper 'dew point' curve (the temperature at which a vapor of that composition starts to condense), enclosing a lens-shaped region between them. Raoult's Law is the physical rule generating that lower curve — each component's partial vapor pressure equals its mole fraction in the liquid multiplied by its own pure vapor pressure at that temperature — and Dalton's Law then says the mixture boils once those partial pressures sum to the surrounding atmospheric pressure. Reading the diagram is how you predict a distillation's outcome without running it: draw a horizontal 'tie line' at the boiling temperature of a given liquid composition, and where it crosses the upper dew-point curve tells you the composition of the vapor in equilibrium with that liquid — always richer in the more volatile component than the liquid it came from, which is the entire reason distillation separates anything at all. A single simple-distillation pass takes you along one such tie line; a fractionating column's packing material provides many small re-condensation-and-re-vaporization surfaces stacked on top of each other, each one repeating that same tie-line step (condense the vapor, let it partially re-boil, draw a new tie line from the resulting liquid), so climbing the column is literally climbing a staircase across the diagram toward the pure, more-volatile corner. This is also exactly where azeotropes reveal themselves visually: at the azeotropic composition, the bubble-point and dew-point curves pinch together and touch, meaning the tie line at that point has zero length — liquid and vapor compositions are identical, and the staircase simply stops climbing.

guides.title: Adhesives, Inks, Dyes & Useful Compounds
guides.summary: How to make glues, inks, and dyes from first principles — the chemistry of adhesion, protein and starch glues, iron-gall and carbon inks, natural dyeing with mordants, and handy household compounds.

sections.heading: How Adhesives Work: Adhesion vs Cohesion
sections.body:
An adhesive joins two surfaces, called the substrates, and it does so through two separate forces that must both hold. Adhesion is the attraction between the glue and the surface it is stuck to, and it has two components acting at once. The first is mechanical interlocking: a liquid glue flows into pores, scratches and cut fibre ends, hardens in place, and becomes thousands of microscopic anchors gripping the material. The second is molecular attraction, the short-range van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds that only operate when glue and surface sit within a fraction of a nanometre of each other. Cohesion is a different thing entirely: it is the internal strength of the hardened glue holding itself together. A joint is only as strong as whichever of the two is weaker, which makes the way a joint breaks the most useful diagnostic available. If the glue peels away clean and leaves one face bare, adhesion failed, and the fix is better surface preparation or a glue matched to that material. If the glue tears down its own middle and leaves film on both faces, cohesion failed, and the fix is a stronger adhesive, a thinner glue line, or a longer cure before loading the joint.

Before either force can act, the glue must wet the surface, spreading into a thin continuous film instead of beading into droplets. Beading signals a surface that is either low in energy or contaminated, usually by oil from skin, silicone or wax, and no amount of clamping pressure rescues a joint that never wetted.

Adhesives harden by one of three mechanisms, and knowing which one you have tells you what the joint needs. Solvent loss means water or another solvent evaporates or soaks into a porous substrate, leaving the dissolved solids behind as a film; white glue, starch paste and rubber cement all work this way, and all of them need at least one porous surface or a long open cure, which is why they fail between two sheets of glass. Chemical curing means two or more components react and cross-link into a rigid polymer network, as in epoxy and cyanoacrylate; these need no porosity and bond metal, glass and plastic. Thermal set means the adhesive melts when hot and solidifies on cooling, as with hot-melt sticks and animal glue, which gels as it cools before it finishes drying.

Surface preparation is not an optional refinement. Degrease with alcohol or acetone, abrade to roughly 120 to 180 grit to raise a mechanical key, wipe off the dust, and bond within minutes, because a freshly abraded metal surface starts re-oxidising immediately. Clamp firmly enough to bring the parts into intimate contact and squeeze out the excess. For most non-gap-filling glues a thin, starved glue line is genuinely stronger than a thick one, because the cured adhesive is weaker than the wood or metal around it, so less of it in the joint means less weak material. The honest exception is the gap-filling adhesives, thickened epoxy and polyurethane foam glue among them, which carry real strength in bulk and are the right choice when the fit is poor.

sections.heading: Making Protein and Starch Glues
sections.body:
Starch paste and animal glue are the two oldest working adhesives in continuous use, and both remain the correct choice for particular jobs rather than mere historical curiosities.

Starch paste sets by drying, but it only becomes glue at all because of gelatinisation. Raw starch granules are tightly packed crystalline bundles that shrug off cold water entirely. Heated in water past roughly 60 to 75 degrees Celsius, depending on the plant source, those granules swell, rupture, and release long amylose chains that entangle into a viscous, sticky network. This is exactly why the flour or cornstarch must be dispersed in cold water first, about one part starch to one part cold water, worked smooth with no lumps, before it goes into three to five parts boiling water. Tipping dry starch straight into hot water gelatinises the outside of each clump instantly and seals raw powder inside, producing the familiar lumpy paste that never reaches full strength. Simmer two to three minutes with constant stirring until the mixture turns translucent, since that colour change is the visible marker that gelatinisation has finished. Cool it before use. It excels on paper, papier-mache and bookbinding because it soaks into fibre and dries flexible, and it is genuinely reversible with water, which is why conservators still reach for it. It is also food, so it grows mould within days; a pinch of salt, a few drops of clove oil, or refrigeration extends its life, and a sour smell means throw it out.

Hide glue and plain gelatin are both hydrolysed collagen. Soak the granules in cold water at roughly one part glue to one and a half parts water for thirty to sixty minutes until fully swollen, then warm gently in a double boiler and hold the temperature between 55 and 65 degrees Celsius. Never let it boil. Heat above about 70 degrees, or several hours held hot, cuts the protein chains shorter and permanently reduces the glue's strength, and that loss is not recovered by cooling it down again. Applied hot to both surfaces it grabs quickly as it gels on cooling, then hardens fully as the water leaves. It is reversible with heat and moisture, which is precisely why furniture and instrument makers prize it, since a joint can be taken apart a century later without destroying the parts. Glue is graded by gram strength, with higher numbers gelling faster and harder, and a cold workshop shortens the open time drastically, so warm the wood before you spread it.

Casein glue uses milk protein and cures genuinely water-resistant. Curdle skimmed milk with vinegar or lemon juice, strain and rinse the curds, then dissolve them in a small quantity of alkali, traditionally slaked lime although borax or washing soda also works. The alkali breaks apart casein's clustered micelle structure and converts the crumbly curd into a smooth sticky liquid. Use it within a few hours, because it thickens and dies in the pot. Slaked lime is caustic, so wear gloves and eye protection, and always add the solid to the water rather than the reverse.

sections.heading: Making Inks: Carbon and Iron-Gall
sections.body:
Any ink is three things at once: a colorant, a liquid vehicle that carries it onto the page, and usually a binder that fixes it there once the vehicle has gone. The distinction that governs everything else is pigment against dye. A pigment is insoluble and merely suspended, so it sits on the surface as discrete solid particles and generally resists light and water extremely well. A dye is dissolved, so it penetrates fibre and flows smoothly from a pen, but it is far more prone to fading in light and to running when wet.

Carbon ink is the pigment case, and it is the most lightfast writing ink known; carbon manuscripts two thousand years old are still legibly black. The pigment is lampblack, essentially pure elemental carbon, collected as soot on a cold surface such as a plate or spoon held in the smoky tip of a candle or oil-lamp flame. Carbon is chemically inert, which is precisely why it never fades. Being inert, it also will not bond to paper by itself, so it needs a binder: gum arabic, a hardened tree exudate, dissolved at roughly one part gum to two parts water. The soot has to be ground into that gum solution rather than merely stirred, because dry soot is strongly agglomerated and water-repellent; grinding breaks the clumps apart and coats each particle so it stays suspended instead of settling out as sludge. A drop of honey or glycerin acts as a humectant and stops the dried film from cracking away, and a trace of clove oil discourages mould. The real weaknesses are honest ones: a poorly bound carbon ink smudges when rubbed, and on very smooth or coated paper the film can flake off because there is nothing for it to key into.

Iron-gall ink is the other great tradition and dominated European writing for more than a thousand years. It combines gallotannic acid, extracted from oak galls, with iron(II) sulfate, historically called green vitriol. Strong black tea, oak bark or sumac leaves substitute for galls at lower tannin concentration. Mixed together, the two form a soluble and almost colourless iron-gallate complex, which is why fresh writing looks pale grey-blue on the page. Atmospheric oxygen then oxidises the iron from its ferrous state to its ferric state over the following hours and days, producing a deep black insoluble pigment locked in among the paper fibres. That progressive darkening is what makes the ink permanent and difficult to erase or alter.

You can improvise the iron by steeping rusty iron or steel wool in vinegar for a week and straining the liquor, but the caveat deserves stating plainly: that liquid has an unknown and variable iron concentration. Add it to the tannin extract a little at a time, watching the colour deepen, and stop while the mixture is still tannin-rich. Stir in gum arabic as the binder. Err always toward too little iron rather than too much, because excess free iron is what eventually destroys the paper the writing sits on.

sections.heading: Natural Dyeing and the Role of Mordants
sections.body:
A dye differs from a pigment in one decisive respect: a dye dissolves and is taken up into the fibre itself, associating chemically with the polymer chains, whereas a pigment sits on the surface held there by a binder. That is why dyed cloth keeps its drape while painted cloth stiffens. Natural dyes come from plant roots, bark, leaves and hulls, from insects such as cochineal, and from a few minerals.

Most natural dyes bond weakly to fibre on their own, and the difference between a colour that survives washing and one that rinses out in the first sink is almost always the mordant. The word comes from the Latin mordere, to bite. A mordant is a metal salt the fibre absorbs first; its ions sit along the fibre as coordination sites, and the dye molecule binds to the metal, bridging dye to fibre. That bridge delivers colourfastness, and because the metal becomes part of the coloured complex, the mordant also shifts the final hue. Alum, potassium aluminium sulfate, is the safest and most widely used, giving clear bright colours close to the dye's own shade, at 10 to 20 percent of the fibre's dry weight. Iron, as ferrous sulfate, saddens colours instead: it darkens and greys them, pushing yellows toward olive and browns toward grey-black, and 2 to 4 percent is ample. Iron also embrittles fibre over time, so restraint there is structural rather than aesthetic. Tannin is used on cotton, linen and hemp as a first step before alum, because cellulose lacks the amine and carboxyl groups wool and silk offer and so has few natural sites for a metal ion to attach to; the tannin supplies them.

The sequence is scour, mordant, extract, dye, rinse. Scouring means washing the fibre in hot water with unscented detergent to strip spinning oils, sizing and factory finish, any of which block uptake and cause blotches. Mordanting means simmering the wetted fibre in the mordant solution at 70 to 90 degrees Celsius for about an hour and then letting it cool in the bath, since a slow cool lets the metal ions distribute evenly rather than crash onto the outer surface. Extraction means simmering the dye material thirty to sixty minutes and straining out the solids. Dyeing means holding the wet mordanted fibre near 80 degrees for thirty to sixty minutes, longer and hotter giving deeper colour.

With wool the felting risk is real but often misdiagnosed: felting comes from rapid temperature change and agitation, not from heat itself, so change temperature gradually and stir slowly rather than avoiding warmth. A worked example: scour 100 grams of wool, mordant with 15 grams of alum for an hour, simmer 40 grams of dry onion skins for 45 minutes and strain, then hold the wool at 80 degrees for 45 minutes for a warm golden yellow that survives washing. The honest caveat is that washfastness and lightfastness are separate properties. Many natural colours, especially berry and other anthocyanin sources, fade badly in sunlight no matter which mordant you use; the genuinely lightfast natural dyes are a short list: madder, weld, indigo, cochineal and the tannin browns.

sections.heading: Handy Household Compounds and Reactions
sections.body:
A handful of simple reactions produce genuinely useful materials from ordinary supplies, and each is worth understanding mechanically rather than as a recipe followed blindly.

Plaster of Paris is calcium sulfate hemihydrate, made industrially by heating natural gypsum to about 150 degrees Celsius to drive off three quarters of its bound water. Adding water puts that water back, and the material recrystallises into a dense mat of interlocking gypsum needles, which is where the strength comes from. Use roughly two parts plaster to one part water by weight, and sprinkle powder into water rather than pouring water onto powder, which traps dry lumps. The set is exothermic and the mould warms noticeably; expect five to eight minutes of workable time, an initial set in twenty to thirty minutes, and full strength only after it has dried for days. Never rinse plaster down a drain; it sets just as happily inside the pipe.

Casein plastic is the same milk protein used for glue, taken further. Warm milk, curdle it with vinegar, strain and knead the curd, then press it into a mould and dry it slowly over several days. The result is a hard, bone-like bioplastic that was genuinely commercial for buttons and beads. Industrial production hardened it with formaldehyde, which is not worth attempting at home; the untreated version is simply more brittle and less water-resistant.

Oxygen bleach is sodium percarbonate, a solid adduct that carries hydrogen peroxide bound to sodium carbonate. Dissolved, it releases both, so you get a peroxide bleach plus an alkaline washing soda in one powder. It needs warm water, ideally 40 to 60 degrees, because below about 30 it barely activates and appears not to work. It is colour-safe because peroxide attacks the coloured chromophores of a stain far less indiscriminately than hypochlorite does, and it decomposes to nothing worse than water, oxygen and soda ash.

Iron acetate is made by steeping degreased steel wool in vinegar for three to seven days with the lid resting loose, since hydrogen is produced and a sealed jar builds pressure. Strained and brushed onto a tannin-rich wood such as oak, walnut or chestnut, it turns the surface grey-black within seconds, and that reaction is exactly the iron and tannin chemistry of iron-gall ink happening on wood instead of paper. On a low-tannin wood such as pine it barely registers, so brush on strong black tea first and let it dry.

Limewash is slaked lime, calcium hydroxide, thinned with water. It hardens by absorbing carbon dioxide from the air and reverting to calcium carbonate, effectively turning back into limestone over weeks to months, which gives a breathable, mildly antimicrobial finish thanks to its pH near 12.4. That same alkalinity makes it caustic to skin and eyes, so gloves and goggles are not optional. Rosin flux works on a related principle of controlled chemical attack: the mild acid in pine rosin becomes active at soldering temperature and strips the invisible oxide film that otherwise stops molten solder wetting the metal, then goes inert again on cooling, which is why rosin residue is safe to leave and acid flux is not.

sections.heading: Safety, Preservation & Common Mistakes
sections.body:
Most of the hazards in this kind of work are chemical burns, poisoning by mistake, and inhaled dust, and all three are avoidable with a few consistent habits.

Anything involving lime, lye or a strong acid is corrosive rather than merely irritating, meaning it destroys tissue on contact and keeps working until it is diluted away. Wear nitrile gloves and eye protection, and always add the solid or the concentrate to the water rather than the reverse. That rule exists because dissolving these materials releases heat, and a small amount of water dropped onto a large amount of caustic or acid can flash to steam and spit the chemical back at your face, whereas the reverse direction spreads the same heat through a large thermal mass harmlessly. If a caustic does reach skin or eyes, flush with running water for a full fifteen minutes by the clock rather than the few seconds that instinct suggests.

Iron sulfate, alum and most other mordants are toxic if swallowed. Label every container clearly, store them away from food and out of reach of children, and dedicate your dye and mordant pots permanently to that use. A pot that has held a mordant should never go back to cooking, because metal salts adsorb into scratches and seasoning and are not reliably scrubbed out. Fine soot and lampblack are a respirable dust, so collect and grind them with ventilation and avoid raising a cloud. Never bring protein glues to a boil, since heat above roughly 70 degrees Celsius permanently shortens the protein chains and the lost strength does not return on cooling.

Preservation is mostly a matter of accepting that water-based glues and inks are food for microbes. Make small batches deliberately, refrigerate what you keep, and add a few drops of clove oil or a pinch of salt to slow spoilage. A sour or yeasty smell means the batch is done, and using it anyway gives a weak bond that fails later for no visible reason. Iron-gall ink largely preserves itself because it is acidic, but keep it capped, since uncontrolled oxidation in an open bottle thickens it and drops sludge.

The common failures follow a short pattern. A joint that peels apart clean almost always means contaminated or unprepared surfaces, since oil and dust block adhesion completely. A glue that will not hold or will not spread is usually a ratio error, too thin to build a film or too thick to soak in and wet the surface. Dyeing without a mordant gives colour that looks convincing wet and rinses away in the first wash, because nothing is bridging dye to fibre. Over-mordanting with iron gives beautiful greys on cloth that tears within a few years. Too much iron in iron-gall ink produces writing that slowly eats through its own page. Failing to clamp a curing adhesive leaves gaps that no glue strength compensates for. Underlying most of these is a single mismatch: use starch for paper, hide or casein for wood, and reserve the reactive adhesives such as epoxy and cyanoacrylate for tough non-porous materials where water-based glues cannot work at all.

sections.heading: Gathering Your Adhesive, Ink & Dye Workshop Kit
sections.body:
The kit behind this work is small, but two of its choices matter far more than they appear to. Vessels should be stainless steel or enamel rather than aluminium or bare iron, because dye work is metal chemistry from start to finish: an aluminium pot quietly mordants the bath for free, and an iron one saddens every colour toward grey. A chemically neutral pot is the only way to be confident that the mordant you weighed out is the mordant actually acting on the fibre. A gram scale matters for the same reason, since nearly every dose here is a percentage of the dry weight of the fibre rather than a spoonful, and ten percent of forty grams is four grams, a quantity no measuring spoon resolves honestly.

Gloves and eye protection are about staining and irritation rather than drama, and dedicating equipment permanently to craft use is about the fact that metal salts lodge in scratches and seasoning and are not reliably scrubbed out. Check fibre content before buying anything you intend to dye, because polyester and most synthetics will not take natural dyes at all, and a blend emerges a pale, patchy version of whatever the pure wool beside it did.
ingredients: A couple of old, non-reactive pots or double-boiler inserts kept exclusively for craft chemistry, not returned to food use — stainless steel or enamel, not aluminum, since some dye and mordant chemistry reacts with aluminum cookware.
A digital kitchen scale and a set of measuring spoons for accurate small-quantity dosing, since many of these recipes are sensitive to ratio.
Nitrile or rubber gloves and basic eye protection, since mordants, iron sulfate, and concentrated dye liquors can stain or irritate skin and eyes.

Powdered alum (potassium aluminum sulfate) and iron sulfate (ferrous sulfate), the two most common natural-dye mordants, sold at craft/fabric or dye-supply stores and some garden centers (iron sulfate also doubles as a lawn/soil amendment).
Gum arabic and/or plain gelatin, both used as binders in traditional ink-making, sold at art-supply and craft stores or, for gelatin, any grocery store.
Tannin-rich plant material — oak galls if you can source them from a nature/craft supplier, or a strong black tea as a widely available tannin substitute.
Natural dye material — onion skins, avocado pits/skins, black walnut hulls, or a purchased natural dye extract (madder, cochineal, indigo) from a fiber-arts or dye-supply shop.
White vinegar and baking soda, both from a grocery store, for the acid-base household reactions and as gentle pH adjusters throughout.

Plain white flour or cornstarch for starch-based glues, and plain (unflavored, unsweetened) gelatin or hide glue granules for protein-based glues, both from a grocery store or a woodworking/craft supplier for the hide glue.
Undyed, prewashed natural-fiber fabric or yarn (cotton, wool, or linen) as your dye test material — synthetic fibers largely won't take natural dyes, so check the fiber content before you start.
Good ventilation or an outdoor workspace whenever you're heating dye baths or mordant solutions, since some give off odors best not concentrated indoors.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Dyeing a Batch of Fabric with Onion Skins and Alum
sections.body:
